title: Nourishing the Parent
reflection: What is one small thing that nourishes me which has slipped away, and who could I reach out to about it?

questions.q: According to Lesson 10, where do the qualities a parent gives, such as peace, patience and kindness, come from?
o: They are gathered from others over the years and then passed to the child.
They come from temperament, and some parents are simply given more of them.
They are made by an effort of will at the moment they are needed.
They are already there in the Self, and practice uncovers them, step by step.
questions.e: Practice is a staircase, and as we climb, the treasures already hidden in the Self come forth more and more: peace and purity, inner beauty and knowledge, compassion, kindness and the spirit of sacrifice. The qualities are not added from outside; they are uncovered. These are the true gifts a parent can give.
questions.c: Practice uncovers the qualities already within; they are the true gifts a parent gives

questions.q: Alone at half past ten at night, a tired parent thinks, “Am I even a good enough mum?” Which view fits Lesson 10?
o: Her tiredness shows that her well is empty, and no more can be asked of her tonight.
The thought is a verdict, and she should answer it with a plan for doing better tomorrow.
She is a divine being whose light is covered by tiredness, and the staircase is still there.
The thought will pass if she lists everything she has done for her daughter today and this week.
questions.e: On that Sunday night she was not a failing mother staring at an empty well. She was a divine being whose light had been covered by tiredness, with the staircase still under her feet. It is a hard thing to believe at once, and honesty about that is a good first step.
questions.c: A tired parent is a divine being whose light is covered

questions.q: In the picture of electric current, what is the ego, and what does the parent’s love become when the ego is quieter?
o: The ego is the wire, and the love is made by the wire when the current runs.
The ego is a resistance, and a lower resistance lets more of divine love flow through.
The ego is the switch, and love flows only when the parent has chosen to turn it on.
The ego is a fuse, and it should be removed so that no love is held back.
questions.e: The ego acts like a resistance in the path of divine energy: the lower the resistance, the greater the flow. The love is fully the parent’s to feel and give, and nothing is taken from it; only its source turns out to be greater than she thought. The parent’s part is to keep the instrument clear.
questions.c: The ego is a resistance; the lower the resistance, the greater the flow

questions.q: On a morning when she is irritable and wants things done her own way, a parent notices that kindness is not flowing. Which step fits Lesson 10?
o: Press on harder, so that kindness is produced by sheer effort and steady discipline.
Ask what resistance is in the way; rest first if the body is just tired.
Treat the irritation as a sign that she is not really suited to parenting at all.
Put the matter aside, and give it no thought at all until the evening practice comes.
questions.e: Some days the instrument will seem blocked. These are the moments to look within and ask what is obstructing the flow: a little ego, strong likes and dislikes, a touch of selfishness. Not every block is ego, though. Sometimes it is simply a tired body, and then rest comes first; that too is care of the instrument.
questions.c: When the flow is blocked, ask what resistance is in the way

questions.q: “A parent who sets aside an hour to sit quietly or to sing is taking that hour from her children, and so is being selfish.”
questions.e: A parent takes up disciplined practice to gain qualities that can then be shared with those in her care. No one can share a treasure they have never gathered. Think of a young person who trains for years to become a doctor: no one calls that selfish, because its end is unselfish service.
questions.c: Caring for oneself as an instrument is no more selfish than a doctor’s training

questions.q: A father loses his poise at bath time with a four-year-old. Which view of the moment fits Lesson 10?
o: It is proof that he does not yet have the qualities of a good parent.
It is feedback, pointing to something that needs more work, and not a failure.
It is a lapse best forgotten quickly, so that it does not weigh on him.
It was caused by the child, and his own part in it is small.
questions.e: Whatever makes us lose our poise and balance in the midst of action and service is feedback, pointing to the places that need more work. These moments are not failures; they are teachers. A parent can receive their own reactions as feedback, and even be grateful to their children for revealing them.
questions.c: Our reactions are feedback, not failure

questions.q: “When a parent’s practice lapses for a week, the earlier days of practice have been wasted.”
questions.e: There will be times when practice lapses under the demands of parenting. Even so, a habit of regular practice, held together with alertness, gradually builds strength. You begin again, and the habit grows a little deeper each time.
questions.c: Begin again: the habit grows deeper each time

questions.q: A parent’s anxiety and low mood have not lifted for several weeks. Which step fits Lesson 10?
o: Add a morning meditation, and expect the mood to lift as the practice settles.
Reach out for help and speak to her doctor; this is part of caring for herself.
Keep going until the children are older, and look after herself then.
Treat it as feedback from her reactions, and work on it in her evening practice.
questions.e: Reaching out for help is part of caring for yourself. If anxiety or low mood doesn’t lift for weeks, or a parent feels low after a birth, she should speak to her doctor. Practice and a circle of support sit beside that care, and do not replace it.
questions.c: Reaching out for help is part of caring for yourself

questions.q: What changes in a parent’s relationship with her child when she sees herself as a trustee and not an owner?
o: She loves the child a little less, and keeps a lighter hold on the family as a whole.
She carries less responsibility, since the Divine is the one who looks after the child in the end.
Clinging gives way to the quiet joy of a caretaker who serves the Divine in the child.
She hands more of the care to others, so that the child grows up in several different homes.
questions.e: A parent is a trustee, given the care of the Divine who has come into the family in the form of a child. Possessiveness, clinging and attachment give way to the quiet joy of a caretaker. Parenting is still full of joy and sacrifice, patience, love and affection, but without the bonds.
questions.c: A trustee, not an owner: care without possessiveness

questions.q: A parent whose circle of friends has thinned has no one to talk to late at night. Which view fits Lesson 10?
o: The strength is within, so turning to others is only a way of avoiding practice and effort.
Strength also comes through others: reach out to one person, or a parents’ circle.
She should wait until her friends’ families have more free time to give her a call.
The lessons themselves can be her circle, and they are enough on their own for her now.
questions.e: The highest source is within us, but the same strength also comes to us through others: parents who share our ideal, a spiritual community and a teacher, other parents, grandparents and the wider family. Those who were helped become helpers. That is one reason this course points to the Ritam Yarning Circle for Parents.
questions.c: A circle of others: the strength also reaches us through people
